lessons.title: Rules
lessons.scenario: Smarty shows Mia and Sam the rules on the notice board outside the town hall.

items.example: You must be on time for school.
items.note: Say 'You must' to tell someone that a rule is very important and they have to follow it.

items.example: You mustn't take a photo in the museum.
items.note: Say 'You mustn't' to tell someone that an action is not permitted at all.

items.example: You are allowed to ride a bike in the park.
items.note: Use 'You are allowed to' when the rules say yes to an action.

items.example: You are not allowed to use a phone in the library.
items.note: Use 'You are not allowed to' to explain politely that a rule says no.

items.example: It is forbidden to make a campfire in the forest.
items.note: Say 'It is forbidden' for a strict official rule that nobody may break.

items.example: It is against the rules to use a phone in the exam.
items.note: Say 'It is against the rules' when an action breaks the rules of a place or game.

grammar.title: must, mustn't, and allowed to
grammar.explanation: Use must for strong rules you have to follow. Use mustn't, not allowed to, forbidden, or against the rules when something is not permitted. Remember that mustn't means do not do it.
examples: You mustn't use a phone in the library.
You are allowed to take a photo outside.

practice.prompt: A rule says wearing a helmet is necessary. Choose the right phrase.
practice.answer: You must
practice.explanation: Use 'You must' when a rule tells you to do something important.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: You mustn't use a phone in the library.
practice.answer: You mustn't use a phone in the library.
options: You mustn't use a phone in the library.
You must use a phone in the library.
You are allowed to use a phone in the library.
practice.explanation: 'You mustn't' means eating in the library is not permitted.

practice.prompt: Match each phrase with its meaning.
practice.explanation: 'Allowed to' gives permission, while 'forbidden' and 'against the rules' say an action is not permitted.

practice.prompt: The park lets people ride bikes here. Complete the sentence.
practice.text: ___ ride a bike in the park.
practice.answer: You are allowed to
practice.explanation: Use 'You are allowed to' when an activity is permitted.

practice.prompt: Dogs cannot enter the museum. Complete the sentence.
practice.text: ___ bring a dog in the museum.
practice.answer: You are not allowed to
practice.explanation: Use 'You are not allowed to' when the rules say no.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence about a strict rule in the forest.
practice.answer: It is forbidden to make a campfire.
practice.explanation: Start with 'It is forbidden' followed by 'to' and the verb.

practice.prompt: Build the sentence about breaking an exam rule.
practice.answer: It is against the rules to use a phone.
practice.explanation: 'It is against the rules' means the action breaks a rule.

practice.prompt: Say the rule aloud.
practice.text: You must take your rubbish home.
practice.answer: You must take your rubbish home.
practice.explanation: Use 'You mustn't' to tell people not to drop rubbish.

story.hook: What rules do Mia and Sam find outside the town hall?

image.describe: Smarty the black cat pointing with his paw at a wooden notice board with picture symbols outside a classic town hall building while Mia and Sam look on.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Look at this notice board, Mia and Sam. It shows every new regulation for the park.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Let me read the first sign. You mustn't leave rubbish on the grass.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And look at the next rule. It is forbidden to make a campfire near the trees.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: What about my bicycle? Do I need permission to ride here?

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: No! You are allowed to ride a bike on the path, but you must be careful.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Good! And you are not allowed to play loud music after nine o'clock because it is against the rules.

questions.prompt: What is forbidden near the trees?
questions.explanation: Sam says: It is forbidden to make a campfire near the trees.

questions.prompt: What are you allowed to do on the path?
questions.explanation: Smarty says: You are allowed to ride a bike on the path.

questions.prompt: Why are you not allowed to play loud music after nine o'clock?
questions.explanation: Sam says it is against the rules to play loud music after nine o'clock.

mission.setup: Smarty asks you to explain the rules at a library and a park.

turns.smarty: Welcome to the library! Tell me one rule about food or phones.
accept: ^you (?:must not|mustn t|are not allowed to) (?:eat|use a phone)(?: in the library)?$
^it is (?:forbidden|against the rules) to (?:eat|use a phone)(?: in the library)?$
turns.example: You are not allowed to use a phone in the library.
turns.hint: Use 'You mustn't', 'You are not allowed to', or 'It is forbidden'.

turns.smarty: Good! Now tell me something people can do in the park.
accept: ^you are allowed to (?:ride a bike|walk|run|play)(?: in the park)?$
turns.example: You are allowed to ride a bike in the park.

turns.smarty: And what strong rule must everyone follow when riding a bike?

lessons.title: Have to
lessons.canDo: Use have to and don't have to
lessons.scenario: Smarty explains to Tom and Mia which tasks at the town hall are necessary and which are optional.

items.example: I need to do my homework before dinner.
items.note: Say 'I need to' when something is necessary for you to do.

items.example: You do not have to pay for a library card.
items.note: Use 'You do not have to' when there is no obligation and you can say yes or no.

items.example: Do I have to bring my passport to the bank?
items.note: Ask 'Do I have to…?' to check if an action is required.

items.example: We had to wait at the station for a long time.
items.note: Use 'had to' to talk about something that was needed in the past.

items.example: Tomorrow I will have to get up early.
items.note: Use 'will have to' to talk about something that will be needed tomorrow.

items.example: You can come with us or stay home. It is up to you.
items.note: Say 'It is up to you' to tell someone that the choice is completely theirs.

grammar.title: have to, do not have to, had to, will have to
grammar.explanation: Use have to or need to when something is necessary. Use do not have to when there is no obligation—it is optional. For past obligations use had to, and for future obligations use will have to.
examples: Do I have to sign here?
You do not have to come early.
Tomorrow we will have to leave at eight.

practice.prompt: The public library is free. Which sentence is right?

options: You do not have to pay.
practice.explanation: 'You do not have to' means something is not required.

options: Do I have to bring my passport?

practice.explanation: 'Do I have to…?' asks if something is necessary.

practice.prompt: Match each phrase with the right time or meaning.

pairs.right: you can say yes or no

practice.explanation: 'Had to' is past, 'will have to' is future, and 'It is up to you' gives free choice.

lessons.title: Local problems
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Omar walk through town noting local problems to report to the council.

items.example: The police station works every day to stop crime.
items.note: Use 'crime' to talk about illegal actions like stealing that break the law.

items.example: There is too much litter near the river.
items.note: Use 'litter' for paper, bottles, and rubbish left on the ground in public places.

items.example: We were late because of a big traffic jam.
items.note: A traffic jam is a long line of cars and buses moving very slowly or not moving at all.

items.example: New shops in town help with unemployment.
items.note: Use 'unemployment' when many people in a town cannot find a job.

items.example: Our charity gives warm food to homeless people.
items.note: Use 'homeless' to describe people who do not have a home to live in.

items.example: A big traffic jam makes air pollution worse.
items.note: Use 'air pollution' for dirty smoke and gas in the air from traffic and factories.

lessons.title: So and such
lessons.scenario: Smarty, Zara, and Leo react to the busy preparations inside the town hall.

items.example: We worked all day, so I am so tired now.
items.note: Put 'so' before an adjective like 'tired' to make the feeling much stronger.

items.example: Smarty is such a nice friend to everyone.
items.note: Use 'such a' before an adjective and a singular noun, like 'such a nice day'.

items.example: There are so many people at the town hall now.
items.note: Use 'so many' before countable plural nouns like 'people' to mean a very large number.

items.example: The new public library is such good news for our town.
items.note: Use 'such' without 'a' before uncountable nouns like 'news' or plural nouns.

items.example: There are too many things on this small table.
items.note: Say 'too many' when there is a bigger number of things than you want or need.

items.example: We have so much to do before the meeting.
items.note: Say 'so much to do' when you have a huge amount of work or tasks ahead.

grammar.title: so vs. such
grammar.explanation: Use so before an adjective alone (so tired), and so many or so much before nouns. Use such before a noun phrase (such a nice day, such good news). Use too many when the number is more than you want.
examples: I am so tired after work.
It was such a nice surprise.
There are so many people here.

practice.prompt: Choose the right phrase before 'neighbour' (an adjective + singular noun).
practice.answer: such a nice
practice.explanation: Use 'such a' before an adjective and a singular countable noun: 'such a nice neighbour'.

practice.audio: The new park is such good news for our town.
practice.answer: The new park is such good news for our town.
options: The new park is such good news for our town.
The new park is so tired now.
There are too many people in the park.
practice.explanation: 'News' is uncountable, so we say 'such good news' without 'a'.

lessons.title: Complaints
lessons.scenario: Smarty helps Mia make a polite formal complaint at the town hall.

items.example: I would like to complain about the litter in the park.
items.note: Start a polite formal complaint with 'I would like to complain about…'.

items.example: It is not acceptable to leave rubbish next to the school.
items.note: Say 'It is not acceptable' when a problem is too bad to ignore.

items.example: This has happened before, and it is still a problem.
items.note: Say 'This has happened before' to show that a problem keeps coming back.

items.example: I expect the council to clean the park soon.
items.note: Say 'I expect' to state clearly and firmly what action should happen next.

items.example: We need to find a solution to the traffic jam.
items.note: Ask for 'a solution' when you want a clear answer or fix for a problem.

items.example: I am afraid that the problem is getting worse.
items.note: Use 'I am afraid that' as a polite way to introduce bad news or a problem.

practice.prompt: How do you start a polite formal complaint at the town hall?

lessons.title: Town meeting
lessons.scenario: Smarty chairs a lively town meeting in the town hall where neighbours vote on community proposals.

items.example: Excuse me, may I say something about the new park?
items.note: Ask 'May I say something?' to join a meeting or discussion politely.

items.example: I would like to add that we need more trees too.
items.note: Say 'I would like to add' when you want to give one more idea after someone speaks.

items.example: We have heard every idea, so let us vote now.
items.note: Say 'Let us vote' when it is time for everyone in a meeting to choose together.

items.example: I agree with the proposal to build a new public library.
items.note: Say 'I agree with the proposal' to support a plan that someone has suggested.

items.example: The majority of people in the room voted yes.
items.note: Use 'the majority' to mean more than half of the people in a group.

items.example: Could we hear from Sam before we vote?
items.note: Ask 'Could we hear from…?' to invite another person in the meeting to share their view.

episode.title: The Secret Behind the Town Hall Clock

panels.speaker: Smarty
panels.text: What a great town meeting! The majority voted to restore the old town hall and public library.

image.describe: Smarty the black cat smiling in the empty town hall meeting hall after the crowd leaves, holding a broom.

panels.speaker: Mia
panels.text: We enlisted to lend a hand with cleaning the upstairs room near the manager office.

image.describe: Mia and Sam carrying a wooden box up a stone staircase inside the town hall.

panels.speaker: Sam
panels.text: I am so tired, and there is still so much to do! Look—what is behind this tall bookshelf?

image.describe: Sam pointing behind a dusty wooden bookshelf in an upstairs town hall room, revealing a small old door.

panels.speaker: Smarty
panels.text: Look at the old sign on that door! It says: It is forbidden to enter without permission.

image.describe: Smarty the black cat inspecting an old wooden door with a brass lock and a faded symbol sign.

panels.speaker: Mia
panels.text: Here comes the mayor! May I say something? We found this locked door behind the shelf.

image.describe: A friendly cat wearing a ceremonial chain smiling as Smarty, Mia, and Sam show the hidden door.

panels.speaker: Smarty
panels.text: The mayor has the spare key! Inside is an ancient box left by the first town council a hundred years ago.

image.describe: The cat mayor unlocking the door while Smarty, Mia, and Sam peek inside at an old wooden chest.

panels.speaker: Sam
panels.text: Such good news! Inside the box there is a faded map of a secret tunnel under the town hall!

image.describe: Smarty, Mia, and Sam leaning over an open wooden chest holding a rolled ancient map with a compass symbol.

panels.speaker: Smarty
panels.text: Where does this tunnel go? We will have to follow the map tomorrow!

image.describe: Smarty the black cat holding a torch and looking excitedly at a stone stairway leading down beneath the town hall.
